subproblems.title: An embedded C¹ m-submanifold of ℝ^P is Borel and countably m-rectifiable (Simon 3.1.2, "if" part)
subproblems.statement: Let P, m ∈ ℕ and let N ⊆ ℝ^P be an embedded m-dimensional C¹ submanifold in the sense of the contract (IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m N): every y ∈ N has an open V ⊆ ℝ^m, an open W ⊆ ℝ^P with y ∈ W and a map ψ : ℝ^m → ℝ^P that is C¹ on V and injective on V, with ψ(V) = W ∩ N, V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) compact for every compact K ⊆ W, and Dψ(z) injective for every z ∈ V. Then N is a Borel set (MeasurableSet N) and N is countably m-rectifiable (CountablyRectifiable m N, the SimonGMT form of Simon Ch. 3, 1.1).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P m : ℕ) (N : Set (Euclid P)), IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m N → MeasurableSet N ∧ CountablyRectifiable m N
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. Simon Ch. 3, Lemma 1.2, "if" part (chapter-03.txt lines 25–34): "if N is an n-dimensional C¹ submanifold, then using local representations for N as in Remark 4.4 of Ch. 2 we see that for each x ∈ N there is ρₓ > 0 such that B_{ρₓ}(x) ∩ N = ψ(V) for suitable C¹ map ψ : V → ℝ^{n+ℓ}, V ⊂ ℝⁿ open. Since such C¹ maps are automatically Lipschitz in each closed ball ⊂ V it is then clear that M satisfies the definition 1.1." In the parent proof these are the facts "N is Borel (SimonGMT measurableSet_of_isSimonSubmanifold, unfolding the contract's chart conditions into IsSimonSubmanifold)" (step 1) and "the embedded C¹ submanifold N′ is countably m-rectifiable (SimonGMT countablyRectifiable_of_isSimonSubmanifold)" (step 7), together with the parent's Lean note on the conversion IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m N → IsSimonSubmanifold (E := Euclid m) 1 N. Here they are stated once for an arbitrary embedded C¹ submanifold; the parent applies them to N and to N′ = Φ(N). Both conclusions are proved in the pinned SimonGMT library (Poincare/SimonGMT/Chapter03/SubmanifoldCover.lean) for SimonGMT's predicate IsSimonSubmanifold, so the proof consists of converting the contract's chart condition into that predicate.

Proof.
1. (SimonGMT's predicate.) Put E := ℝ^m = Euclid m. By definition (Poincare/SimonGMT/Chapter02/Submanifold.lean), IsSimonSubmanifold (E := E) 1 N means: 1 ≤ 1 in ℕ∞, and for every y ∈ N there are V ⊆ E, W ⊆ ℝ^P and ψ : E → ℝ^P with y ∈ W and IsSimonLocalRepresentation 1 N V W ψ. The latter is the conjunction: V is open; W is open; ψ is C¹ on V (ContDiffOn ℝ (1 : ℕ∞) ψ V); ψ is injective on V; ψ(V) = W ∩ N; IsProperOnInto ψ V W, i.e. for every K with IsCompact K and K ⊆ W the set V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) is compact; and Dψ(z) is injective for every z ∈ V.
2. (Conversion.) The condition 1 ≤ 1 holds by reflexivity. Let y ∈ N. The hypothesis IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m N supplies V, W, ψ with: V open; W open; y ∈ W; ContDiffOn ℝ 1 ψ V, where 1 is the natural number 1; ψ injective on V; ψ(V) = W ∩ N; for every K ⊆ W with IsCompact K, the set V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) is compact; and Dψ(z) injective for every z ∈ V. These are exactly the clauses of step 1, up to two purely formal differences:
 - the smoothness order: the natural number 1 and (1 : ℕ∞) have the same image in the smoothness-order type used by ContDiffOn, so the two ContDiffOn statements are the same proposition (in Lean: by exact_mod_cast);
 - the properness clause: IsProperOnInto ψ V W takes the hypotheses "IsCompact K" and "K ⊆ W" in the other order, so it is obtained by swapping them.
 Hence IsSimonSubmanifold (E := Euclid m) 1 N.
3. (Borel.) By SimonGMT measurableSet_of_isSimonSubmanifold applied to step 2, N is a measurable, i.e. Borel, set. (Its proof: the chart neighbourhoods W_y, y ∈ N, cover N, and ℝ^P is hereditarily Lindelöf, so countably many of them, W_j, cover N; each W_j ∩ N = ψ_j(V_j) is the continuous image of the σ-compact open set V_j, hence σ-compact and Borel; so N = ⋃_j (W_j ∩ N) is Borel.)
4. (Countably rectifiable.) By SimonGMT countablyRectifiable_of_isSimonSubmanifold applied to step 2, CountablyRectifiable m N. (Its proof is Simon's argument quoted above, in compact-exhaustion form: with the countable chart cover of step 3, each W_j ∩ N = ψ_j(V_j); the open set V_j is a countable union of compact sets C_{j,k} ⊆ V_j; ψ_j is C¹, hence locally Lipschitz, on a neighbourhood of each point of V_j, so it is Lipschitz on each compact C_{j,k}; each such restriction extends to a Lipschitz map ℝ^m → ℝ^P (finite-dimensional Lipschitz extension, Simon Ch. 2, 1.2); so W_j ∩ N is contained in a countable union of Lipschitz images of ℝ^m (SimonGMT countablyRectifiable_image_contDiffOn_open), and a countable union of countably m-rectifiable sets is countably m-rectifiable.)
5. Steps 3 and 4 give MeasurableSet N ∧ CountablyRectifiable m N. ∎

subproblems.title: Signed change of variables: a nonnegative area formula transfers integrable real integrands
subproblems.statement: Let α, β be types with σ-algebras, μ a measure on α, ν a measure on β, Φ : α → β, A ⊆ α, B ⊆ β, J : α → ℝ with J(x) ≥ 0 for every x, and f : β → ℝ. Assume the nonnegative change-of-variables identity ∫⁻_B g dν = ∫⁻_A ofReal(J(x))·g(Φ(x)) dμ(x) holds for every function g : β → [0, ∞]. If f is ν-integrable on B (Integrable f (ν.restrict B)) and x ↦ J(x)·f(Φ(x)) is a.e.-strongly measurable for μ⌞A, then x ↦ J(x)·f(Φ(x)) is μ-integrable on A and ∫_B f dν = ∫_A J(x)·f(Φ(x)) dμ(x).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (α β : Type) [MeasurableSpace α] [MeasurableSpace β] (μ : Measure α) (ν : Measure β) (Φ : α → β) (A : Set α) (B : Set β) (J : α → ℝ) (f : β → ℝ), (∀ x, 0 ≤ J x) → (∀ g : β → ℝ≥0∞, ∫⁻ y in B, g y ∂ν = ∫⁻ x in A, ENNReal.ofReal (J x) * g (Φ x) ∂μ) → Integrable f (ν.restrict B) → AEStronglyMeasurable (fun x => J x * f (Φ x)) (μ.restrict A) → Integrable (fun x => J x * f (Φ x)) (μ.restrict A) ∧ ∫ y in B, f y ∂ν = ∫ x in A, J x * f (Φ x) ∂μ
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source. Parent step 11: "Apply (3.1) with B₀ = B to g = ofReal∘f and g = ofReal∘(−f): since J ≥ 0, ∫_{C′} ofReal(±f) dH^m = ∫_B ofReal(J(x))·ofReal(±f(Φ(x))) dH^m = ∫_B ofReal(±h_ω) dH^m. Writing the integrals of the integrable functions f (on C′) and h_ω (on B) as differences of the integrals of their positive and negative parts (integral_eq_lintegral_pos_part_sub_lintegral_neg_part), …", abstracted from the data (C′, B, J, f, H^m) to arbitrary data. The integrability of J·(f∘Φ), which the parent obtained in step 10, is derived here from the same identity applied to g = |f|. This is the standard passage from the nonnegative area formula (Simon Ch. 2, 3.5 and 4.13, chapter-02.txt lines 788–797 and 975–981, stated there for non-negative functions) to integrable real-valued functions.

Notation. ν_B := ν⌞B = ν.restrict B and μ_A := μ⌞A = μ.restrict A; F(x) := J(x)·f(Φ(x)); for t ∈ ℝ, ‖t‖ₑ = |t| ∈ [0, ∞) is its extended norm and ofReal t = max(t, 0) ∈ [0, ∞), so that ofReal(t) and ofReal(−t) are the positive and negative parts of t.

Proof.
1. (The hypothesis.) (H): for every g : β → [0, ∞], ∫⁻ g dν_B = ∫⁻ ofReal(J(x))·g(Φ(x)) dμ_A(x). No measurability of g is required by (H), so it may be applied to any of the functions below.
2. (Integrability of F.) For every x, ‖F(x)‖ₑ = ‖J(x)‖ₑ·‖f(Φ(x))‖ₑ (extended norm of a product, enorm_mul), and ‖J(x)‖ₑ = ofReal(J(x)) because J(x) ≥ 0 (Real.enorm_of_nonneg). Applying (H) to g := (y ↦ ‖f(y)‖ₑ):
 ∫⁻ ‖F‖ₑ dμ_A = ∫⁻ ofReal(J(x))·‖f(Φ(x))‖ₑ dμ_A(x) = ∫⁻ ‖f‖ₑ dν_B < ∞,
 the last inequality because f is ν_B-integrable (finite integral of its extended norm). So F has finite integral for μ_A; together with the hypothesis that F is a.e.-strongly measurable for μ_A, F is μ_A-integrable. This is the first conclusion.
3. (Positive parts.) Applying (H) to g := ofReal∘f gives
 ∫⁻ ofReal(f) dν_B = ∫⁻ ofReal(J(x))·ofReal(f(Φ(x))) dμ_A(x) = ∫⁻ ofReal(F(x)) dμ_A(x),
 because ofReal(a)·ofReal(b) = ofReal(a·b) whenever a ≥ 0 (ENNReal.ofReal_mul), applied pointwise with a = J(x) ≥ 0.
4. (Negative parts.) Applying (H) to g := ofReal∘(−f) gives

 - M ⊆ ℝ^P: trivial;
 - M is countably m-rectifiable: hypothesis;
 - θ is measurable (a constant function) and θ(y) = 1 > 0 for every y ∈ M;

subproblems.statement: Let P, n ∈ ℕ, U ⊆ ℝ^P, and R = (M, θ, ξ) an IMRep of U (Simon 6.3.1 data). Then there is T ∈ 𝒟_n(U) such that T(ω) = R.action ω = ∫_M θ(x)⟨ω(x), ξ(x)⟩ dHⁿ(x) for every ω ∈ 𝒟ⁿ(U) (R.Represents T). Here T ∈ 𝒟_n(U) means a GeometricCurrentOn U n: a linear functional on 𝒟ⁿ(U) with T(ω_j) → 0 whenever ω_j → 0 in Simon's test-form topology (TestFormOnConverges).

Source: Simon 6.3.1 (chapter-06.txt lines 733–753), where formula (‡) is asserted to define a current. The parent proof uses this in step 6.6 for X̃ = τ(M_X ∩ K, θ_X, ξ_X) in U.
Notation: μ := Hⁿ⌞M = μHE[n].restrict M; for a covector α, ‖α‖ is its operator norm as a continuous alternating map.
1. Unit orientations have norm at most one. By the field orients, for μ-a.e. x there are a subspace Q and an orthonormal family τ = (τ₁, …, τₙ) such that ξ(x)(α) = α(τ) for all α, or ξ(x)(α) = −α(τ) for all α (IsUnitOrientationOf). Then for every covector α, |ξ(x)(α)| = |α(τ₁, …, τₙ)| ≤ ‖α‖·∏ᵢ|τᵢ| = ‖α‖ (ContinuousAlternatingMap.le_opNorm; the product is empty when n = 0).
2. Measurability. For every continuous n-form ω, the function x ↦ θ(x)ξ(x)(ω(x)) is μ-a.e. strongly measurable. Indeed θ is measurable (ℕ-valued), ξ is μ-a.e. strongly measurable (field aestronglyMeasurable_orient), ω is continuous, and evaluation (L, α) ↦ L(α) is continuous because it is bounded bilinear (isBoundedBilinearMap_apply; Continuous.comp_aestronglyMeasurable₂).
3. θ is integrable over compact sets. Let K be compact with K ⊆ U. Then 1_K θ is μ-integrable: it is measurable, and ∫ 1_K θ dμ = ∫_{M∩K} θ dHⁿ < ∞ by the field locallyIntegrable_mult, since (Hⁿ⌞M)⌞K = Hⁿ⌞(K ∩ M) (Measure.restrict_restrict; integrable_indicator_iff). Write C_K := ∫ 1_K θ dμ ∈ [0, ∞).
4. Integrability of the integrand. Let ω ∈ 𝒟ⁿ(U), K := tsupport ω (compact, ⊆ U), and B := sup_y ‖ω(y)‖ < ∞ (ω is continuous with compact support). By step 1, for μ-a.e. x, |θ(x)ξ(x)(ω(x))| ≤ θ(x)‖ω(x)‖ ≤ B·1_K(x)θ(x); if x ∉ K then ω(x) = 0. By steps 2–3 and domination (Integrable.mono'), x ↦ θ(x)ξ(x)(ω(x)) is μ-integrable.
5. Linearity. Define T(ω) := R.action ω for ω ∈ 𝒟ⁿ(U). Each ξ(x) is linear, so the integrand for ω + η is the sum of the integrands for ω and η. Both are integrable by step 4, so T(ω + η) = T(ω) + T(η) (integral_add). The integrand for cω is c times the integrand for ω, so T(cω) = cT(ω) (integral_const_mul). Thus T is a linear functional on 𝒟ⁿ(U), and R.Represents T holds by definition.
6. Sequential continuity. Let ω_j → 0 in 𝒟ⁿ(U) (TestFormOnConverges ω_j 0). Then there is a compact K ⊆ U with tsupport ω_j ⊆ K for all j, and every derivative converges uniformly on K. For the 0-th derivative (‖D⁰g(x)‖ = ‖g(x)‖ and D⁰0 = 0) this says ε_j := sup_{x∈K} ‖ω_j(x)‖ → 0. By step 1, for μ-a.e. x, |θ(x)ξ(x)(ω_j(x))| ≤ ε_j·1_K(x)θ(x), since ω_j(x) = 0 off K. Hence |T(ω_j)| ≤ ε_j·C_K (norm_integral_le_of_norm_le with step 3). Given ε > 0, choose N such that ‖ω_j(x)‖ < ε/(C_K + 1) for all j ≥ N and x ∈ K. Then |T(ω_j)| ≤ εC_K/(C_K + 1) < ε for j ≥ N, so T(ω_j) → 0.
7. By steps 5 and 6, T is a GeometricCurrentOn U n with T(ω) = R.action ω for every ω ∈ 𝒟ⁿ(U). ∎

For a test form ω the integrand is a.e. strongly measurable and dominated by sup|ω|·1_{spt ω}·θ, which is integrable by local integrability of θ. Hence ω ↦ ∫_M θ⟨ω, ξ⟩ dHⁿ is linear.
If ω_j → 0 in 𝒟ⁿ(U) with supports in a compact K, then |T(ω_j)| ≤ sup_K|ω_j|·∫_{M∩K} θ → 0, so T is a current.

Hence for ω ∈ 𝒟ⁿ(U) the functions θ ξ(ω) … are bounded a.e. on C by θ ‖ω‖_∞ 1_{tsupport ω} … and are integrable on C'). This makes explicit the absolute convergence of the integral in Simon Ch. 6, 3.1 (‡) (chapter-06.txt lines 733–745), where θ is locally Hⁿ-integrable and ξ = τ₁ ∧ ⋯ ∧ τₙ with τ orthonormal.

1. (Test-form data.) ω ∈ TestFormOn U n means IsTestForm f ∧ tsupport f ⊆ U (ω.2.1 and ω.2.2). IsTestForm f means ContDiff ℝ ∞ f and HasCompactSupport f. Hence:

   - K is compact and closed, hence measurable, and K ⊆ U;
   - f(x) = 0 for x ∉ K (image_eq_zero_of_notMem_tsupport).
   By Continuous.bounded_above_of_compact_support there is B ∈ ℝ with ‖f(x)‖ ≤ B for all x. Here ‖·‖ is the operator norm on Covector (Euclid P) n = (Euclid P) [⋀^Fin n]→L[ℝ] ℝ.

2. (Pointwise bound for ξ.) By the field R.orients, for μ⌞C-a.e. x there are a subspace Q and τ : Fin n → ℝ^P with Orthonormal ℝ τ such that either ξ(x)(α) = α(τ) for all n-covectors α, or ξ(x)(α) = −α(τ) for all α.
   - For every α, ContinuousAlternatingMap.le_opNorm gives ‖α(τ)‖ ≤ ‖α‖·∏_i ‖τ_i‖.
   - ∏_i ‖τ_i‖ = 1, since ‖τ_i‖ = 1 for each i (first component of Orthonormal). For n = 0 the product is empty and equals 1.
   - Hence |ξ(x)(α)| = |α(τ)| ≤ ‖α‖ for all α (use abs_neg in the second case).
   So for μ⌞C-a.e. x, |ξ(x)(α)| ≤ ‖α‖ for every α.

3. (Measurability.)
   - x ↦ (θ(x) : ℝ) is measurable: θ is measurable and every function on ℕ is measurable (measurable_from_nat composed with R.measurable_mult).
   - The evaluation map MultiVector P n × Covector (Euclid P) n → ℝ, (φ, α) ↦ φ(α), is continuous (Continuous.clm_apply applied to continuous_fst and continuous_snd).
   - x ↦ (ξ(x), f(x)) is a.e. strongly measurable for μ⌞C: pair R.aestronglyMeasurable_orient with the continuous f using AEStronglyMeasurable.prodMk.
   - Hence x ↦ ξ(x)(f(x)) is a.e. strongly measurable (Continuous.comp_aestronglyMeasurable), and so is F (AEStronglyMeasurable.mul).
   Formalization note: applying ContinuousLinearMap.aestronglyMeasurable_comp₂ to ContinuousLinearMap.apply ℝ ℝ fails to unify the topology instance on MultiVector P n. Composing with the continuous evaluation map, as above, works.

4. (Integrable dominating function.) Let g(x) := B * K.indicator (fun x => (θ x : ℝ)) x, i.e. g = B·1_K·θ.
   - x ↦ (θ(x) : ℝ) is integrable on K for μ⌞C. It is measurable by step 3. Its lower integral is ∫⁻_K ‖(θ(x) : ℝ)‖ₑ d(μ⌞C) = ∫⁻_{K∩C} θ dμ = ∫⁻_{C∩K} θ dμ, using Measure.restrict_restrict (K measurable) and ‖(k : ℝ)‖ₑ = (k : ℝ≥0∞) for k ∈ ℕ (hasFiniteIntegral_iff_enorm).
   - This lower integral is ≠ ∞ by R.locallyIntegrable_mult K, since K is compact and K ⊆ U.
   - Hence K.indicator θ is integrable for μ⌞C (IntegrableOn.integrable_indicator, K measurable), and so is g (Integrable.const_mul).

5. (Domination.) Let x be one of the a.e. points of step 2.
   - If x ∈ K: |F(x)| = θ(x)·|ξ(x)(f(x))| ≤ θ(x)·‖f(x)‖ ≤ θ(x)·B = g(x), using θ(x) ≥ 0, step 2 and step 1.
   - If x ∉ K: f(x) = 0, so F(x) = θ(x)·ξ(x)(0) = 0 = g(x).
   Thus ‖F(x)‖ ≤ g(x) for μ⌞C-a.e. x.

6. (Conclusion.) Integrable.mono' applies: g is integrable (step 4), F is a.e. strongly measurable (step 3), and the a.e. bound holds (step 5). Hence F is integrable for μ⌞C = μHE[n].restrict R.carrier. ∎

R.orients gives ξ(x) = ±(α ↦ α(τ)) with τ orthonormal a.e. on C, so |ξ(x)(α)| ≤ ‖α‖ by le_opNorm and ∏‖τ_i‖ = 1.

It is dominated a.e. by B·1_K·θ, which is integrable because ∫⁻_{C∩K} θ dHⁿ < ∞ (locallyIntegrable_mult).

subproblems.title: Euclidean coefficient-norm duality for unit simple n-vectors (Cauchy–Binet)
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P n : ℕ), ∃ L : MultiVector P n →L[ℝ] Covector (Euclid P) n, ∀ (ξ : MultiVector P n) (Q : Submodule ℝ (Euclid P)), IsUnitOrientationOf ξ Q → (∀ α : Covector (Euclid P) n, |ξ α| ≤ covectorEuclideanNorm α) ∧ covectorEuclideanNorm (L ξ) ≤ 1 ∧ ξ (L ξ) = 1
subproblems.natural_proof:
Reused comparator-accepted declaration (DAG node root.density_one_implies_regular-a1.imrep_mass_and_support-a1.unit_orientation_duality-a1, status accepted, frozen Lean type byte-identical). Its independently reviewed proof is reproduced below; there, 'the parent proof' and 'sibling' refer to that node's own branch.
Source: step 1 of the parent proof (Simon Ch. 6, §1: coordinate covectors dx^I and the pairing of Λⁿ with Λₙ). The Cauchy–Binet identity is proved inline.
Notation:
- e_0, …, e_{P−1} is the standard basis of ℝ^P (EuclideanSpace.basisFun), and v(i) is the i-th coordinate of v ∈ ℝ^P.
- Λⁿ := Covector (Euclid P) n, the continuous alternating n-linear maps (ℝ^P)^n → ℝ; Λₙ := MultiVector P n = Λⁿ →L[ℝ] ℝ.
- 𝓘 is the finite set of strictly increasing I : Fin n → Fin P, and e_I := (e_{I(0)}, …, e_{I(n−1)}).
- For α ∈ Λⁿ, |α| := covectorEuclideanNorm α = (Σ_{I ∈ 𝓘} α(e_I)²)^{1/2}. The defining sum runs over all I : Fin n → Fin P, with term α(e_I)² for strictly increasing I and 0 otherwise, so it is the same sum.
- For v = (v_0, …, v_{n−1}) ∈ (ℝ^P)^n and I ∈ 𝓘, v^I is the n×n matrix with (k, j) entry v_j(I(k)).
1. (Coordinate covectors.) For I ∈ 𝓘 let dx^I ∈ Λⁿ be dx^I(v) := det(v^I). It is n-linear and alternating in v, because the determinant is multilinear and alternating in its columns and column j, (v_j(I(k)))_k, depends linearly on v_j. It is continuous because ℝ^P is finite-dimensional. In SimonGMT (Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter06.FormsDuality), dx^I = wedgeCovectors n (fun k ↦ EuclideanSpace.proj (I k)), and wedgeCovectors_apply_det gives exactly this formula. For n = 0, dx^I is the constant covector 1, the determinant of the empty matrix.
2. (Kronecker property.) For I, J ∈ 𝓘, dx^I(e_J) = 1 if I = J and dx^I(e_J) = 0 if I ≠ J. The matrix (e_J)^I has (k, j) entry 1 if I(k) = J(j) and 0 otherwise. If I = J it is the identity matrix. If I ≠ J, the ranges differ, because a strictly increasing map Fin n → Fin P is the increasing enumeration of its range. Both ranges have n elements, so some I(k) is not in range J. Row k of (e_J)^I is then zero, and the determinant is 0.
3. (Expansion.) For every α ∈ Λⁿ and v ∈ (ℝ^P)^n: α(v) = Σ_{I ∈ 𝓘} α(e_I)·dx^I(v).
 Both sides are alternating n-linear functions of v; the right side is a linear combination of the dx^I. By multilinearity, two n-linear maps on ℝ^P agree once they agree on every basis tuple e_f := (e_{f(0)}, …, e_{f(n−1)}), f : Fin n → Fin P.
 - If f is not injective, both alternating maps vanish at e_f, which has a repeated entry.
 - If f is injective, let J ∈ 𝓘 enumerate range f increasingly, and let σ be the permutation of Fin n with f = J ∘ σ. By alternation, each side at e_f equals sign(σ) times its value at e_J. At e_J the right side is Σ_I α(e_I) dx^I(e_J) = α(e_J) by step 2.
 Hence the two sides agree.
4. (Sum of squared minors; Cauchy–Binet.) For every orthonormal family τ = (τ_0, …, τ_{n−1}) in ℝ^P, Σ_{I ∈ 𝓘} det(τ^I)² = 1. This is the Cauchy–Binet formula det(AᵀA) = Σ_I det(A_I)² for the P×n matrix A with columns τ_j, where AᵀA = Id. Self-contained derivation:
 - Let δ_τ ∈ Λⁿ be δ_τ(v) := det(⟨τ_i, v_j⟩)_{i,j}. It is n-linear, alternating and continuous for the same reasons as dx^I, and equals wedgeCovectors n (fun i ↦ ⟨τ_i, ·⟩).
 - By orthonormality, δ_τ(τ) = det(⟨τ_i, τ_j⟩) = det(Id) = 1.
 - δ_τ(e_I) = det(τ_i(I(j)))_{i,j} = det((τ^I)ᵀ) = det(τ^I), and dx^I(τ) = det(τ^I).
 - Step 3 with α = δ_τ and v = τ gives 1 = δ_τ(τ) = Σ_I δ_τ(e_I)·dx^I(τ) = Σ_I det(τ^I)².
5. (Proof of (a).) Let ξ, Q satisfy IsUnitOrientationOf ξ Q, with orthonormal τ and sign s, so ξ(α) = s·α(τ) for all α. For α ∈ Λⁿ, step 3 and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in ℝ^𝓘 give
 |ξ(α)| = |α(τ)| = |Σ_I α(e_I) det(τ^I)| ≤ (Σ_I α(e_I)²)^{1/2}·(Σ_I det(τ^I)²)^{1/2} = |α|·1,
 using step 4.
6. (Definition of L.) For ζ ∈ Λₙ put L(ζ) := Σ_{I ∈ 𝓘} ζ(dx^I)·dx^I. Each ζ ↦ ζ(dx^I) is evaluation at a fixed point, a continuous linear functional on Λₙ. So L is a finite sum of continuous linear maps Λₙ → Λⁿ, i.e. L ∈ (MultiVector P n →L[ℝ] Covector (Euclid P) n). For example, L = Σ_I (ContinuousLinearMap.apply ℝ ℝ (dx^I)).smulRight (dx^I). L does not depend on ξ.
7. (Coefficients of L(ζ).) For J ∈ 𝓘, step 2 gives L(ζ)(e_J) = Σ_I ζ(dx^I)·dx^I(e_J) = ζ(dx^J). Hence |L(ζ)|² = Σ_{J ∈ 𝓘} ζ(dx^J)².
8. (Proof of (b) and (c).) For ξ as in step 5, ξ(dx^J) = s·dx^J(τ) = s·det(τ^J).
 - By step 7 and step 4, |L(ξ)|² = Σ_J s²·det(τ^J)² = 1, so |L(ξ)| = 1 ≤ 1.
 - By linearity of ξ, ξ(L(ξ)) = Σ_I ξ(dx^I)·ξ(dx^I) = Σ_I det(τ^I)² = 1.
9. (Degenerate cases need no separate treatment.)
 - For n = 0, 𝓘 consists of the empty map, e_∅ is the empty tuple, dx^∅ = 1 and |α| = |α(e_∅)|. Steps 1–8 hold verbatim.
 - If n > P, then 𝓘 = ∅ and step 4 would give 0 = 1. So ℝ^P has no orthonormal family of n vectors, the hypothesis IsUnitOrientationOf ξ Q never holds, and the statement is vacuous (L = 0).
proof_key_steps: Define dx^I(v) = det(v_j(I(k)))_{k,j} (SimonGMT wedgeCovectors of coordinate projections); dx^I(e_J) = δ_IJ for strictly increasing I, J.
Expansion α(v) = Σ_I α(e_I)·dx^I(v): both sides are alternating multilinear and agree on all basis tuples.
Σ_I det(τ^I)² = 1 for orthonormal τ (Cauchy–Binet), by expanding δ_τ(v) = det(⟨τ_i, v_j⟩) at v = τ.
Cauchy–Schwarz gives |ξ(α)| = |α(τ)| ≤ |α|.
L(ζ) = Σ_I ζ(dx^I)·dx^I is continuous linear, with |L(ξ)|² = Σ_I det(τ^I)² = 1 and ξ(L(ξ)) = Σ_I det(τ^I)² = 1.

subproblems.statement: Let P, n be natural numbers, U ⊆ ℝ^P, R = (M, θ, ξ) : IMRep U n, and ω ∈ 𝒟ⁿ(U) (TestFormOn U n: a C^∞ n-form on ℝ^P with compact support and tsupport ω ⊆ U). Source: step 2 of the parent proof (Simon Ch. 6, 3.1 (‡) and 3.2(3)). The parent bounds the integrand with the Euclidean bound of its step 1. Here the same bound is used in operator-norm form, which avoids the Cauchy–Binet computation.
Notation: M = R.carrier, θ = R.mult, ξ = R.orient, ν := μHE[n].restrict M = Hⁿ⌞M, μ := R.measure = ν.withDensity (x ↦ (θ(x) : ℝ≥0∞)), f(x) := ξ(x)(ω(x)), K := tsupport ω. For an n-covector α, ‖α‖ is its operator norm as a continuous alternating map.
1. ω is C^∞, hence continuous, and has compact support. So K is compact, closed and Borel, and K ⊆ U because ω ∈ 𝒟ⁿ(U).
2. θ is measurable (R.measurable_mult; ℕ carries the discrete σ-algebra), so x ↦ (θ(x) : ℝ≥0) is measurable. A measure with a density is absolutely continuous, so μ ≪ ν (withDensity_absolutelyContinuous).
3. (Measurability.) ξ is ν-a.e. strongly measurable (R.aestronglyMeasurable_orient), hence μ-a.e. strongly measurable since μ ≪ ν. ω is continuous, hence strongly measurable. Evaluation Λₙ × Λⁿ → ℝ, (ζ, α) ↦ ζ(α), is continuous (bounded bilinear; isBoundedBilinearMap_apply.continuous). So f is μ-a.e. strongly measurable (Continuous.comp_aestronglyMeasurable₂).
4. (Pointwise bound.)
 - By R.orients, for ν-a.e. x (hence μ-a.e. x) there are an orthonormal family τ and s ∈ {1, −1} with ξ(x)(α) = s·α(τ) for all α. Then |f(x)| = |ω(x)(τ)| ≤ ‖ω(x)‖·∏_j ‖τ_j‖ = ‖ω(x)‖ (ContinuousAlternatingMap.le_opNorm).
 - Since ω is continuous with compact support, there is C with ‖ω(x)‖ ≤ C for all x (Continuous.bounded_above_of_compact_support).
 - If x ∉ K then ω(x) = 0, so f(x) = ξ(x)(0) = 0.
 Hence |f| ≤ C·1_K μ-a.e.
5. (Finiteness.) Since K is measurable, μ(K) = ∫_K θ dν = ∫_{M∩K} θ dHⁿ. This is finite by R.locallyIntegrable_mult, as K is compact and K ⊆ U. So C·1_K is μ-integrable, and by step 3 and domination (Integrable.mono'), f is μ-integrable.
6. (Integral identity.) For measurable g : ℝ^P → ℝ≥0 and any function h, ∫ h d(ν.withDensity g) = ∫ g(x)·h(x) dν(x). This is integral_withDensity_eq_integral_smul and needs no integrability hypothesis. Take g = θ, noting (θ(x) : ℝ≥0∞) = ((θ(x) : ℝ≥0) : ℝ≥0∞). Then
 ∫ f dμ = ∫ θ(x)·f(x) dν(x) = ∫_M θ(x)·ξ(x)(ω(x)) dHⁿ(x) = R.action ω.
 Together with step 5 this proves both claims.
proof_key_steps: f(x) = ξ(x)(ω(x)) is μ_R-a.e. strongly measurable: ξ is, μ_R ≪ Hⁿ⌞M, and evaluation is continuous.
μ_R-a.e. |f| ≤ ‖ω‖ ≤ C·1_{spt ω}, because ξ(x) = ±ev_τ with τ orthonormal.
μ_R(spt ω) = ∫_{M∩spt ω} θ dHⁿ < ∞ by locallyIntegrable_mult, so f is integrable.
∫ f dμ_R = ∫_M θ f dHⁿ = R.action ω by the withDensity integral formula.
